paragraphs.text: Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 is a connective tissue disorder whose features overlap with Marfan syndrome and Loeys-Dietz syndrome. Craniofacial features include hypertelorism and bifid uvula. Skeletal features include arachnodactyly, joint hypermobility, pectus deformity, and either tall stature or growth retardation (Rienhoff et al., 2013; Kuechler et al., 2015). Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) showed that cardiovascular involvement can be significant, including thoracic and abdominal aortic aneurysm and dissection and mitral valve disease. They also noted striking clinical variability both within and between families.

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) described a 9-year-old European American girl born to nonconsanguineous, healthy parents. Birth weight was 2.9 kg (5th centile). At birth she had contractures of the right hand, most severe in the 3rd and 4th fingers, and of all toes. She also had a midline facial nevus flammeus and mild hypotonia. At age 3 months she was evaluated for failure to thrive and delayed gross motor function. At 17 months she weighed 7.5 kg (less than 1st centile) and was 76 cm tall (5th centile). Findings at that age included bilateral pes planus, mild pectus excavatum, hyperextensibility of multiple large joints, mild retrognathia, prominent eyes, hypertelorism, blue sclerae, a small metopic ridge, and a bifid uvula with an intact hard palate. Muscle bulk was decreased in all appendicular and axial muscles, with strength 1/5, low tone, and diminished reflexes, and subcutaneous fat was markedly reduced. She stood independently with a positive Gowers sign at 20 months and walked at 24 months with a 'hip waddle' gait. Her neurocognitive development was appropriate for age. Radiographs showed bilateral coxa valga. At age 7 years she weighed 15.5 kg (less than 1st centile) and was 115 cm tall (5th centile). A quadriceps biopsy at that age showed type 1 fiber predominance with mild, focal type 1 fiber disproportion consistent with disuse. Yearly echocardiograms from 18 months showed no cardiac defect or dysfunction. At 6.5 years, the aortic annulus and aortic root measured 1.34 cm (z score 0.59) and 1.72 cm (z score 0.39), respectively.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) studied a large Dutch family (family 1) whose features overlapped with Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes. Seven family members, aged 40 to 68 years, had aneurysms and dissections, mainly of the descending thoracic and abdominal aorta. Three died from aortic dissection and rupture. Four members had mitral valve abnormalities, ranging from mild prolapse to severe regurgitation that required surgery. Craniofacial abnormalities were subtle and included a long face, high-arched palate, and retrognathia. Pectus deformity and scoliosis were frequent. Other recurrent findings were velvety skin, varices, and hiatal hernia. Several family members had autoimmune features, including HLA-B27-positive spondyloarthritis, Graves disease, and celiac disease.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) summarized the features of 43 patients (23 male, 20 female; median age 34 years) from 11 families with TGFB3 mutations. Vascular involvement ranged from no cardiovascular abnormality at age 64 to type A aortic dissection (median age 51 years, range 40 to 80) or type B aortic dissection (median age 44.5 years, range 30 to 57). It also included abdominal aortic dissection and, in one patient, death from cerebral aneurysm dissection at age 55. The authors observed no early arterial dissection, no dissection at small aortic dimensions, and no striking arterial tortuosity. Other cardiovascular findings were mitral valve disease, persistent foramen ovale, and atrial or ventricular septal defects. Skeletal findings included tall stature (12 patients), arachnodactyly (16), kyphoscoliosis (11), joint hypermobility (9), and pectus deformity (8). Loeys-Dietz features included hypertelorism (14), bifid uvula (11), cleft palate (5), cervical spine instability, and clubfoot. Other recurrent features were dolichocephaly, high-arched palate, retrognathia, and inguinal hernia. Medical records showed no evidence of ectopia lentis, and early-onset osteoarthritis was reported in only 2 individuals. Clinical variability within and between families was striking.
